transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hi Dr. Smith. Nice to meet you. So, um, I guess the main reason I finally made an appointment is because I just feel like I absolutely cannot get my life organized right now, specifically my schoolwork and my little accessories shop that I run. I try to do both at the same time, and I really thought I could handle it, but it’s just turning into a complete disaster. 

Like, my workspace is just this massive mountain of stuff. I have all my shop supplies—like all my little beads, the wire, the bubble mailers, and these tiny little jewelry bags—just completely mixed up with my school stuff. So there are receipts and shipping labels buried under my assignment notes and my printed syllabuses, and I keep missing due dates because I literally can't find the piece of paper that actually says when things are due. Everything just ends up in these huge, overwhelming piles all over my desk, and then it spills onto the floor, and then onto my bed, and I just stand there staring at it all and I honestly don't even know what to do first. 

I'll pick up a receipt to put it away, but then I see a half-finished assignment and think I should probably work on that, but then I realize I need to mail an order out before the post office closes, and it’s just... it’s making me crazy. I really want to do well in my classes and keep my shop going because I love making the accessories, but I just can't seem to keep any of it straight or figure out where to even begin cleaning it up.

Thinking back, did you have similar struggles with organization, focus, or finishing tasks when you were in grade school or high school, or does this feel like a new problem that's developed more recently?

Oh, it is definitely not a new thing at all. Honestly, it's been like this for as long as I can remember, um, probably all the way back to when I was really little. Actually, my mom—she's one of those people who saves absolutely everything, like she has these big plastic bins in the hall closet full of every single thing I ever did in school—she still has all my old elementary school report cards and the little notes my teachers used to send home. 

And it's so crazy to look at them now because they literally all say the exact same things. Every single year, the teachers would write these notes to my parents saying I was always out of my seat. Like, they'd be trying to teach a lesson or we were supposed to be doing silent reading, and I'd just be wandering over to the pencil sharpener or going to look at the bulletin board because I just couldn't stay planted in the chair. 

And they always, always complained that I was talking before being called on. I remember just feeling like if I didn't say the answer right that very second, I was going to explode. So I'd just blurt it out before they even finished asking the question, or I'd talk right over the other kids, which I know drove my teachers completely crazy. 

And then whenever we had group activities, I would just completely rush through them. Like, I actually understood the work! I wasn't rushing because it was too hard and I wanted to get it over with—I usually knew exactly what we were supposed to be doing—but I just could not force myself to go at the same slow pace as the other kids. I just had to get it done, done, done. I'd speed through my part and then start trying to do their parts too, just to make it go faster, because waiting for them felt like physical torture. 

So, yeah, I guess I’ve always been exactly like this. It’s just that back then it was just a nuisance for my teachers, and now it’s literally ruining my business and my college classes, you know? Like, the stakes are just so much higher now, and it feels so much heavier than it did when I was eight and just getting a frowny face sticker on a folder.

Aside from feeling overwhelmed by the disorganization itself, do you find yourself worrying excessively about many different things—like your grades, finances, or relationships—on most days, even when things are going okay?

Honestly, no, not really. I mean, it's actually kind of funny you ask that because my roommate, she is a total worrier. Like, she will sit there and obsess over a text message her mom sent her for three hours, wondering if there's some hidden meaning, or she'll freak out about her bank account even right after she gets paid. And I am just... I'm not like that at all. 

Like, if things are actually going okay? If I somehow miraculously managed to turn in a paper on time and I don't have a huge backlog of shop orders hanging over my head? I am completely fine. I don't sit around borrowing trouble, you know? I don't worry about my relationships—my boyfriend and I are great, and if we ever do have a problem, I just tell him right then and there. I just blurt it out, I don't stew on it. And my finances, well, I mean I'm a college student so I'm obviously not rich, but I don't obsess over money unless I literally don't have enough to buy my bead supplies for the week. 

The only time I feel that really intense, heavy chest, panic kind of feeling is when I am staring directly at the disaster on my desk and realizing I'm about to fail a class because I lost the syllabus, or when a customer emails asking where their package is and I realize I completely forgot to make their bracelet. It's very situational, I guess? Like, it's only a reaction to the actual, physical mess I've made of my schedule and my room. If the mess isn't there, the worry isn't there. I'm usually a pretty upbeat person! I just like doing things and keeping moving, so sitting around just worrying about abstract things isn't really my style. I just only get stressed when a hypothetical problem turns into a real, actual disaster that I caused because I couldn't keep my stuff straight.

latest_inference.note: Childhood onset of hyperactivity, impulsivity, and inattention with clear situational anxiety only related to disorganization rules out GAD (F41.1). No pervasive low mood, anhedonia, or depressive symptoms reported, ruling out F32.9. Symptoms are consistent with ADHD persisting into adulthood.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports lifelong, childhood-onset symptoms of both inattention (chronic disorganization, losing important paperwork/deadlines, difficulty completing tasks in sequence) and hyperactivity-impulsivity (out-of-seat behavior, blurting answers before being called on, inability to wait for turn-taking in group tasks) documented across multiple settings (school records/teacher notes) and currently causing significant functional impairment in both academic and occupational (small business) domains. Symptoms are pervasive rather than episodic, present since early childhood, and not better explained by generalized anxiety (patient explicitly denies pervasive, free-floating worry, describing distress as strictly situational and reactive to disorganization-related consequences). The combination of both inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive symptom clusters supports the Combined Presentation, consistent with ICD-10 F90.0 (Hyperkinetic Disorder, disturbance of activity and attention).
